q: Which aromas are classed as tertiary?
opts: Fresh citrus and green apple from a cool-climate vineyard
Those developed by bottle age and oxidative maturation
Banana from carbonic maceration during fermentation
Vanilla picked up from a new oak barrel
exp: Leather, mushroom and dried fruit are the usual markers, built by bottle age and by slow oxidation in barrel rather than by the barrel's own aroma, which is secondary. Their presence is the strongest evidence for calling an older vintage range.

q: Vanilla, coconut and sweet spice on the nose most often point to what?
exp: Oak lactones and vanillin come from the barrel, while malolactic conversion runs to butter rather than vanilla. American oak tends to the coconut and dill end, French toward finer spice.

q: A buttery aroma in a white wine is most commonly attributed to what?
opts: New oak alone, since barrels give butter too
exp: Diacetyl is the by-product, and a barrel contributes vanilla and spice rather than butter. Whether it is welcome is a style question, and many producers block malolactic to preserve tautness.

q: Why should a taster smell the wine before swirling as well as after?
opts: Swirling oxidises the wine past the point of useful assessment
The most volatile compounds show before agitation
The ritual is traditional and tells the taster nothing
exp: The still nose catches the lightest, most fleeting compounds, and some faults announce themselves there first. Swirling then releases the heavier ones by increasing the surface area.

q: Aroma intensity is assessed independently of quality because what?
opts: Quality is decided on the palate alone, not on the nose
A restrained wine may be fine and a loud one ordinary
exp: Keeping the two apart is the discipline. Many great wines are quiet, particularly when young or served too cold, and the nose contributes to a quality judgement without intensity settling it.

q: Fruit described as fresh rather than cooked or dried suggests what about origin?
opts: A cooler climate or a younger wine
High residual sugar holding the fruit fresh
A warmer climate, where longer hang time keeps the fruit crisp
Extended barrel ageing, which preserves the fruit as it was picked
exp: Fruit condition is one of the better climate clues: crisp and tart at the cool end, baked and jammy at the warm end. Time in barrel dries the fruit character rather than preserving it.

q: Which structural components are assessed on the palate?
opts: Sweetness, acidity, tannin, alcohol and body
Tannin and colour, with the other components left aside
exp: Each is judged separately before any conclusion about balance. Colour and clarity belong to the sight stage and cannot be tasted. Running the components together is how a high-alcohol wine gets called sweet.

q: Length, in tasting terms, refers to what?
opts: How long the bottle has aged before opening
The length of time the bottle stays open
How long the wine spent in barrel before bottling
exp: Persistence is one of the more dependable quality markers, and it is measured in seconds after the wine has been swallowed or spat.

q: A wine described as balanced means what?
opts: No single component dominates the others
It is exactly half sweet and half dry
exp: Balance is a relationship rather than a level: high acid can be balanced by high sugar, and high tannin by fruit and body.

q: Body, in tasting terms, describes what?
opts: The alcohol reading on the label and nothing else
The wine's weight and texture in the mouth
The depth of colour, which tracks how heavy a wine feels
exp: Alcohol, glycerol, sugar and extract all contribute, so no single figure captures it. Whole-mouth impression rather than a single measurable component, and a pale wine can be as weighty as a black one.

q: Perceived sweetness in a dry wine can be created by which component?
opts: High alcohol or ripe fruit character
exp: Alcohol reads faintly sweet and very ripe fruit reads sweeter still. A technically dry wine is regularly described as sweet for this reason.

opts: Smelling the empty glass after the wine has been poured away
Aroma arriving from the back of the mouth
Smelling the wine in the glass before it is swirled
exp: Much of what is called flavour is smell reaching the olfactory receptors from behind. It is why a blocked nose flattens food and wine alike.

q: Why do tasters draw air across the wine in the mouth?
exp: Air lifts the aromatic compounds off the liquid and up behind the palate, which is retronasal perception. Unattractive to watch and genuinely informative.

q: A wine that seems hollow in the middle is usually said to lack what?
exp: Attack and finish present, nothing between. It is a common shape in over-cropped or heavily manipulated wine.

q: Acidity is judged physically by which sensation?
opts: Warmth at the back of the throat
A drying grip on the gums
Salivation at the sides of the tongue
exp: The mouth waters in response to acid, while warmth is the alcohol talking. Counting how long salivation continues is a practical way to rank two wines.

q: Which wine component registers as touch rather than as a taste?
exp: Astringency is touch rather than taste: tannin binding the lubricating proteins in saliva. It is why it builds across several sips.
